title: The World’s Biggest Climate Conference Just Fell Apart
excerpt: If for nothing else, the United Nations’ annual climate gathering can be useful for focusing world leaders’ attention on the fate of the planet for a week or tw
body: If for nothing else, the United Nations’ annual climate gathering can be useful for focusing world leaders’ attention on the fate of the planet for a week or two

During this year’s conference, though, Presidents Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin were instead meeting with one another in China, where they agreed to increase oil production; only one G7 leader, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, showed up in Antalya, Turkey, where the UN conference, known as COP 31, was held
When a world leader did appear at the conference, a media scrum would form, Marek Pruszewicz, a former BBC editor who now runs the climate publication Dialogue Earth , told me
But when the leaders left, reporters seemed to vanish just as quickly
He saw television journalists working amid empty seats and rows of vacant press tables. “It’s just not cutting through,” Pruszewicz said
The same could be said of the year’s biggest climate fight in the United States, over a permitting-reform bill that the Senate passed on Thursday
Proponents argue that the bill is necessary for clean energy to thrive; opponents see it as a gift to gas companies

If you talk with people involved in this debate, or dip into the corners of social media where the issues are being litigated out loud, you’ll still find vehement arguments about the fate of the planet
But it’s hard to shake the feeling that the world seems to care less about solving this problem than it once did
On Sunday, the COP negotiations collapsed for only the third time in the conference’s 30-year history
The world’s diplomats spent more than 20 years at these climate negotiations before they agreed to even mention fossil fuels, the dominant driver of global warming, as part of the problem
That happened five years ago, at the UN climate summit in Glasgow, when negotiators agreed not on a “phase out” but on just a “phase down” of the use of coal

The following year, in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, dozens of countries pressed for an agreement to “phase down” all fossil fuels; only in 2023, in Dubai, did diplomats commit to the more effervescent idea of a “transitioning away.” The negotiations over the past two weeks in Antalya made those past efforts sound ambitious, even idealistic
During the talks this week, negotiators stripped out all references to fossil fuels and to reducing the world’s dependence on them from a draft agreement
The negotiators also cut references to the historical responsibility of developed countries for causing climate change

Mohamed Adow, the director of Power Shift Africa, a climate-advocacy group, told reporters on Friday that this has been “the worst COP ever.” The negotiations ran into overtime, as negotiators tried to land on an agreement that could gain the necessary consensus to pass, but on Sunday, they admitted that they had failed

The signature proposal, set by the host nation at the conference’s outset, was to set a goal of increasing the proportion of electrification of the world’s energy consumption from 23 percent, where it is now, to 35 percent by 2035

This shift is seen as important for eventually lowering carbon emissions, by switching out internal-combusion cars and oil heaters with electric alternatives, which can be more efficient even if their electricity comes from power plants burning fossil fuels

Reaching “35 by 35” would not be easy—it would require a more than fourfold speedup in the pace of electrification—but hitting that goal still wouldn’t keep the atmosphere from warming 2 or more degrees Celsius from the baseline before the Industrial Revolution
That amounts to “catastrophic global warming,” Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told me from Antalya last week

The electrification goal, he said, was, to begin with, a “minor and insufficient consolation.” Ultimately, the negotiations broke down in part over the question of whether the agreement would mention fossil fuels at all
Some environmentalists worry that Congress, too, is too willing to ignore the problem of fossil fuels’ future
The bipartisan permitting bill, which will now head to the House, would rewrite bedrock environmental laws to speed up the build-out of transmission lines and new sources of clean energy

But these laws would also make it easier to build all sorts of infrastructure, including (opponents point out) gas pipelines, data centers, and ICE-detention centers, as well as (proponents note) ecological-restoration projects
Like COP’s organizers, the architects of this bill see it as a practical measure that will continue advancing climate goals
One of its sponsors is Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, who has been one of the most consistent advocates for climate policy in Congress

The bill’s supporters argue that it clears the way for clean energy to continue its takeover, even if, in the short term, the bill also helps the fossil-fuel industry. (Opponents see fossil-fuel companies as better positioned to take advantage of any new build-out.) Some former Biden-administration staffers believe that the bill could fix a problem they ran into with their signature climate legislation: They made it easier to build solar and wind farms, but not easier to build the power lines to connect them to anything
No one thinks that the bill does enough, on its own, to dramatically change the trajectory of U.S. emissions; people on both sides of the argument fear a future in which the status quo sticks
Climate scientists are taking encouragement where they can
If the biggest climate fights of 2027 will be focused on limited “practical” questions, then so will the clearest advances: The use of solar- and other renewable-energy sources is growing
Both are happening far faster in many other countries than they are in the United States
Still, the reminders about the costs of continued warming were hard to miss this year: the glacier collapse in Nepal that swept away more than 1,500 people
The summer heat wave in Europe that killed some 50,000 more
The El Niño in an already overheated Pacific Ocean that’s spinning out droughts and floods around the world

Climate scientists say the goal of keeping warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius will inevitably be surpassed; the latest report by the World Meteorological Organization found that global mean temperatures from January to September were 1.47 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels

Celeste Saulo, the WMO secretary general, told reporters last week that the past dozen years have been the warmest on record, and the past four, including 2026, were the warmest of those. “There is no end in sight,” she said

The question has moved to how bad the “overshoot” period will be and what can be done to minimize the damage and avoid tipping points. “That includes your large ice sheets melting, glaciers melting,” Rachel Cleetus, the climate-program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, told me. “Once that happens, you can’t bring them back.” The mood going into COP was “pretty somber,” she said, in a year when climate disasters have piled up and fossil-fuel companies reported record profits
She had left for Antalya from Boston amid fall temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit
By the time the COP talks ended with little to show, most everyone had gone home, and the mood was grim.

title: Is the Populist Moment Over?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Throughout history, a familiar pattern has shown itself: Political elites lose touch with the people over who
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Throughout history, a familiar pattern has shown itself: Political elites lose touch with the people over whom they rule, and those people rebel in one way or another
But eventually a new kind of elite asserts itself
The rise of Donald Trump as a political force more than a decade ago was part of one such global wave of anti-elite sentiment

If the midterm results signal the end of the Trump era, do they also signal the beginning of the end of our populist moment? In this episode of The Permanent Questions , Fareed Zakaria joins David Brooks to discuss the history of liberal democracy and the inevitable reactions against it, why technology makes this reaction different from others, and the ways in which our liberal elite will have to change if they want to own the future
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Today on The Permanent Questions we’re going to talk about a permanent problem
It is that great nations fall when elites get too distanced from the masses and lose popular legitimacy
Here are some examples: The Roman empire in the fifth century, the French monarchy in the 18th century, the Russian aristocracy in the early 20th century, and the shah’s Iran in 1979
The elites have grown insular and condescending toward the people
The elites break the social contract with the people, and the people withdraw their trust and any sense of legitimacy
It seems to me that the United States and many other societies around the globe have been flirting with this kind of catastrophe for many decades
Millions of people have lost faith in the elites, in institutions, in the future, and in each other
These losses of faith produce populist backlashes, and that’s what we’ve been living through over the past 15 years or so
Populist leaders have arisen in societies across the world
Nations on nearly every continent have their own version of Donald Trump
But it turns out that the populists can be guilty of all the sins people associate with the old elite
In fact, they can be more corrupt, more incompetent, more morally bankrupt, more out of touch than the people they promised to replace
When that happens, the voters want to throw the populace out too, and I believe that’s what happened in the American election of 2026

So the million-dollar questions become: What comes next? Can leaders in either party reform themselves and win back the trust of the people? Can we restore the kind of popular legitimacy that any nation needs to function okay? Most immediately, are we past peak populism? Have the winds shifted so much that a new historical era is possible? And if so, what’s it going to look like? I’ve asked Fareed Zakaria to join as we wrestle with these questions
Fareed is the host of Fareed Zakaria GPS , CNN’s global-affairs show
He writes a weekly column in The Washington Post

He’s the author of many celebrated and influential books, including The Future of Freedom , The Post-American World , In Defense of a Liberal Education , and most recently, Age of Revolutions: Progress and Backlash From 1600 to the Present
He’s one of the most profound thinkers in the world today, and so I’m pleased to welcome Fareed Zakaria to this table
Brooks: Yes, I’m sure it’s the honor of your life
Zakaria: Honestly, to have a conversation with you is a pleasure and an honor
So one of the things I loved about your most recent book, The Age of Revolutions , is that you describe how liberal societies were built in the first place
Some of your examples are the Netherlands and their golden age, the British golden age, America, and some of the others
I thought that might be useful as we think about where we are as liberal societies, and especially where we are in this moment of, I think, rebuilding
Hopefully, an upcoming moment of rebuilding
My point of view, as you know, is that this election was so big that we could say, maybe not globally, but in the U.S. at least, not only is Trumpism over, but we’ve passed peak populism
Now, you have a more global perspective than I do
Do you agree with that? Zakaria: So I think in every way—if you look in the book, every one of these liberal experiments, you tend to see a backlash
At some point people say, “This is too much change
We’re moving too far away from the traditions, the mooring, the community, the old faith of our fathers.” And you get a backlash
Then the question becomes how society handles that backlash
Does it find a way to rebuild, as you say, or does it end up getting mired in a certain kind of dysfunction? The French Revolution being the best example of it not working out

I think where we are is still in that backlash to 30 or 40 years of globalization, massive economic and technological change, enormous cultural change—the rise of women, the rise of minorities, immigration being the kind of symbolic aspect of that change
But I do think you’re right that in America we have now seen something interesting, which is Trump 2.0 was a much more pure implementation of right-wing populism than Trump 1.0
People forget that in the first Trump term, there was a lot of Paul Ryan and Steve Mnuchin and a lot of the old kind of Republican Party still at work
Trump 2 was all populism, and it (a) didn’t work—manufacturing employment is not back in America—and (b) the public didn’t like it
So there is a kind of sense that: Okay, these guys might have been pointing to a problem that was real, but they don’t have the solution

title: The Rise and Fall of the Telephone Century
excerpt: High-tech gadgets proliferated almost as rapidly in Mark Twain’s time as they do in ours, and he prided himself on being an early adopter
body: High-tech gadgets proliferated almost as rapidly in Mark Twain’s time as they do in ours, and he prided himself on being an early adopter

So when Alexander Graham Bell’s new telephone company began to offer service in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1877, Twain signed up, boasting (incorrectly) that his was the first line “ever used in a private house in the world.” Shortly afterward, he did set a record, becoming “the first author to deploy the telephone in fiction, in a peculiar story for The Atlantic Monthly ,” James Gleick writes in The Telephone: A New History

The comedy of “ The Loves of Alonzo Fitz Clarence and Rosannah Ethelton ” comes mainly from its high-concept premise: The title characters fall in love, quarrel, reconcile, and get married entirely over the phone, without ever meeting in person
At the time the story appeared, in March 1878, very few Americans had actually seen a telephone, and Twain plays up the strangeness of the new technology

When we are first introduced to Alonzo, in his study in Eastport, Maine, he seems to be talking to himself, or to someone in the next room, before it’s revealed that he’s actually on the phone with his Aunt Susan in San Francisco
But although Twain found technology fascinating, he also knew that things—even things that do amazing things—don’t make for good stories
The only subject that human beings find enduringly interesting is one another, and Twain was remarkably prescient about how the telephone would challenge traditional terms of interaction

The lovers in Twain’s story are separated by thousands of miles, but the conversation between them is not at either end, nor is it somewhere in the middle; it is a meeting of minds that have escaped the body’s requirement of place
This raises questions that we’re still asking today, in the age of dating apps and OnlyFans

Can people be real to one another without physical presence? Can there be love without touch? “There was a feeble but frantic sound for some little time, as if wool-lipped, disembodied spirits were exchanging kisses,” Twain writes about his telephone lovers
Is that funny or nightmarish? Gleick’s great achievement as a science writer has been to show how complicated, abstract ideas end up changing the way we experience the world
In Chaos , he explored chaos theory, which used new mathematical tools to explain why weather and other complex systems are so unpredictable
In The Information , he showed how modern discoveries such as DNA and the computer involved new ways of thinking about data and communication
The Telephone , too, is the story of a scientific discovery

But it’s just as much the history of a business—the Bell System, a group of companies led by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company (AT&T) that became America’s most powerful and enduring monopoly
The book is also a wide-ranging cultural history, showing how the telephone changed people’s lives and how they tried to make sense of those changes

When Bell gave a public demonstration of his invention in Salem, Massachusetts, speaking with Thomas Watson 18 miles away, in Boston, “it seemed as if an electric thrill went through the audience,” he remembered. “They recognized for the first time—what was meant by the ‘Telephone.’ ” But what did it mean, exactly? That is where novelists like Twain came in—along with playwrights, psychologists, social scientists, and legions of pundits in what Gleick calls the “Telephone Century.” Like artificial intelligence today, the telephone was an obviously momentous new technology that everyone had heard about and no one fully understood
If the parallel holds, we won’t know how AI is going to change the world until after it happens, because early predictions about how people would use the telephone turned out to be wildly off base

A New York Times article imagined it as a way to listen to sermons without having to go to church, joking that soon houses for rent would offer Baptist preachers “laid on in every room,” like hot and cold water
In France, the Théâtrophone service allowed subscribers (including Marcel Proust) to listen to live opera performances over the phone
In both cases, the telephone was viewed as a one-way delivery system
But its power would lie in being a network—literally, a web of metal cables spanning continents and oceans, which allowed any two people, anywhere in the world, to have a back-and-forth exchange
Not even Bell knew at first exactly what he was inventing
The initial goal of his research wasn’t to transmit the human voice, but to increase the carrying capacity of existing telegraph lines by sending multiple messages simultaneously at different pitches
In the course of his experiments with vibrating steel reeds, he discovered the principle that made the telephone possible: Sound and electricity speak the same language
Sound travels through the air in waves of pressure, and electromagnetic force also takes the form of a wave
The telephone was a tool for translating between the two kinds of waves
A small magnet, vibrating in response to a speaking voice, would generate an electrical current, which could be sent down a wire and reconverted into sound at the other end
Bell wasn’t the only person to make this discovery
Philipp Reis had built a device he called das Telephon in Germany in 1861, and Elisha Gray, an American inventor, was so close on Bell’s heels that both men’s applications reached the U.S

Bell was awarded the patent, as well as the chance to go down in history as the inventor of the telephone, mainly because his well-connected Washington lawyer bribed the patent examiner with $100 and a gold watch
Making the new invention useful would be a lot more expensive
As Gleick observes, other Industrial Age enterprises benefited from economies of scale
The more automobiles you make, the cheaper manufacturing each one becomes
With the telephone, the calculation was reversed: The bigger the network, the greater the cost per call, given how many lines and switchboards were required to put all the calls through
Raising capital from ultrarich investors became crucial
Originally Bell was one of four partners in the company that bore his name
Within three years, he had been reduced to one of 540 shareholders and ceased to play any real role
At first, independent telephone companies tried to challenge the Bell System, in business and in court
Some enterprising farmers even turned their barbed-wire fences into telephone lines by running electric current through them

title: The Relationship That Can Survive Not Talking for Years
excerpt: If you don’t speak with a relative for years, you’re probably estranged
body: If you don’t speak with a relative for years, you’re probably estranged
If you’re dating someone who’s dropped contact for the past month, you’ve been ghosted
You haven’t heard from your boss in six months? Uh-oh
But one kind of relationship seems to consistently defy the laws of interpersonal physics: friendship

When friends reunite, the fabric of time can pleat seamlessly, allowing them to simply, as the saying goes, pick up where they left off. “Time doesn’t take away from true friendship, nor does separation,” Tennessee Williams wrote in Memoirs . “When we’re together, the years fall away,” Judy Blume once wrote of her best friend, Mary

In the 100 interviews with groups of friends that I conducted for my series The Friendship Files , I often heard similar sentiments. “It was like we’d never been apart,” one person told me of reconnecting with his Army buddies after more than a decade. “It’s as if nothing has changed,” another said of their relationship with friends from kindergarten
If friendship has a superpower, it is the time travel of reconnection
Before these moments, sometimes weeks, months, or years pass with only sporadic communication, if not complete silence
Yet through these fallow periods, friendship can persist without diminishing in strength
I’ve come to think of these empty spaces as friendship’s dark matter
It is the part of friendship we can’t see, directly measure, or definitively prove exists—but we know it’s there, and we feel its effects

In a 1991 paper , Stuart Sigman, a communication researcher, emphasized the importance of the part of relationships that happens in the silence between interactions. “Relationships do not cease after the face-to-face events (conversations) engaged in by co-members are terminated,” he wrote. “In a sense, relationships are ‘larger’ than the physical presence or interactional accessibility of the participants.” Although all relationships have some of this dark matter, friendship is unusual because of how much silence it can survive
Someone doesn’t necessarily lose the title of “friend” just because you haven’t talked to them in a while
With family or romantic partners, a reunion after a long separation could be expected to bring some drama

Yet seeing an old friend is often described as frictionless. [ Read: How friendships change in adulthood ] The nature of friendship allows for this goodwill. “Freedom lives at the heart of friendship,” William Rawlins, an emeritus professor of communication at Ohio University, told me
You can’t choose your parents, but every friendship is created from scratch by the participants themselves
Cultures have shared expectations for how romantic relationships progress and when families ought to gather
Although couples and families don’t necessarily conform to those scripts, they’re still aware of them
Those cultural guideposts barely exist for friendship

There is no universal prescription for how often friends ought to talk to or see one another. “Our friendship is going to exist as long as we are living up to each other’s expectations of the friendship,” Rawlins said

Friendships can go dormant for a while without dying, he wrote in his 1992 book, Friendship Matters , so long as all parties still think of one another as friends: “The unspoken in friendship, its shared image, may excuse former neglect.” So what is happening when nothing is happening between friends? This is the question Kinneret Lahad, a professor of women’s studies at Tel Aviv University, explored in a paper she published last year

The short answer, as she wrote, is that when nothing happens, “everything happens at the same time.” The full answer is more complicated. “Friendship is imbued with so many sensations, so many intensities that cannot be quantified or qualified or represented in narratives,” Lahad told me. (I’ll try my best to represent some of them in this narrative nevertheless.) Nothing visible or measurable may be happening between two friends; they may be, by all appearances, out of touch
But perhaps they think of each other often
Maybe one helped the other find a job that took them to a new place many years ago; their whole life trajectory remains shaped by that friendship, even though they’re now apart
One friend might see something that makes them think of the other, wonder whether they should reach out, and almost do it, only to hesitate at the last moment

Any or all of that could be happening when a friendship appears dormant. “When nothing is happening in friendship, all of friendship’s ambiguities, possibilities, and constraints are laid bare,” Rawlins said
Lahad’s point is that all of these almosts, maybes, and intangible thoughts still matter
They still affect the friendship and the people within it
This dark matter can, like the universe’s, be the glue that keeps friends together, or it can be the shadows in which misunderstandings and resentments fester
One indirect piece of evidence for the existence of friendship dark matter is that the feeling of closeness between friends is not necessarily linked to how often they are in touch

In a study of long-distance and geographically close friends, Amy Janan Johnson, a professor of communication at the University of Oklahoma, found that although far-flung friends did fewer “maintenance behaviors”—such as calling each other, joking around together, and offering emotional support—that did not mean they felt less connected or invested in the relationship

In fact, she told me, some long-distance friends’ commitment to the relationship was “still increasing.” Johnson suggested that in addition to the active maintenance of talking to and seeing one another, people might also engage in passive maintenance of their friendships by, for instance, looking at old photos and feeling fond feelings, or thinking of someone and wishing them well
These things seem small and ephemeral, but they are ways that friendship can be present even in absence

And they may contribute to the feeling, upon reunion, that the friendship was never interrupted at all. [ Read: Want closer friendships? Move away from your friends. ] Lahad recently published another paper , with her friend and co-author Klara Goedecke, about the feeling of reconnecting after a period of nothingness

And in the most scholarly way possible, they basically said that it’s magic: “Sensed suspension of the sociotemporal order that would otherwise cast time apart as rupture has a ‘mythical’ or ‘extra-temporal’ quality,” they wrote, “which we conceptualize as a sense of wonder.” This wonder is not guaranteed
Let us not over-romanticize the flexibility of friendship; it is completely possible that the dark matter contains not the comforting certainty of continued connection, but confusion and hurt

Friends can drift apart over long separations, and reuniting may be awkward rather than smooth. “Meeting up with an old friend constituted a friendship trial,” Lahad and Goedecke wrote, “a moment where the friendship was put to the test, as it were.” Reconnection comes with risk

Although you may have thought that everything was fine, that it was mutually understood that you still loved each other through the silence, your friend might be upset with you for not reaching out. “Treasured old friendships persist partly as vital (and hopefully mutual) fantasies,” Rawlins wrote
The risk is that the fantasy is not mutual
As technology has made keeping in touch easier and easier, the dark matter of friendship may feel heavier than it did in previous generations

title: How ‘Real Food’ Nearly Broke the White House
excerpt: Kennedy Jr. staged a “policy celebration” at the Department of Health and Human Services headquarters to give an update on one of his signature initiatives: a n
body: Kennedy Jr. staged a “policy celebration” at the Department of Health and Human Services headquarters to give an update on one of his signature initiatives: a new definition of ultra-processed food

Publishing the definition would be the first step toward achieving several “Make America Healthy Again” goals, such as new front-of-package labels to steer consumers away from unhealthy foods and, eventually, a reduction in preventable disease
But even as Kennedy was planning the festivities, a months-long bureaucratic battle was threatening to derail it

Days before the planned event, senior staff at the White House told Kennedy’s team that the definition would need to stay secret because it had not yet cleared a review process at the Office of Management and Budget
That review had become a major point of contention
Some inside the administration wanted more data on the economic effects of policies that could follow from the definition; others insisted that the delay was unnecessary and political
When Kennedy took the stage, flanked by children holding Eat Real Food posters, he could announce only that an announcement was still coming
This dispute over regulatory language has since helped unravel the team that cemented the MAHA-MAGA alliance and has guided Donald Trump for years
Less than two weeks before the midterms, a Kennedy ally named Calley Means quit his job at the White House in protest
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles then mounted a new effort to release the definition before the election, only to have Kennedy pause it
On the same day that Wiles announced her resignation following a poor Republican showing in the midterm election, Means appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast to accuse her of caving to the food industry
Inside the White House, some staff were outraged

One White House official that day called Means a liar and a failure who “confuses his own inability to persuade with others’ malfeasance.” Now, under the new regime of Chief of Staff Stephen Miller—who has long claimed his own special affinity for MAHA—the ultra-processed-food language, a draft of which we obtained, is once again moving forward

According to several people with knowledge of the plan, HHS has been preparing again for a long-awaited release of the definition, which is expected as soon as next week. (When asked for comment, HHS directed us to the White House, which sent a statement that listed past MAHA accomplishments and declared, “Stephen Miller and Secretary Kennedy have been working closely together since day one, and they will continue advancing bipartisan MAHA victories.”) The story of the conflagration at the White House, which involves Trump-administration staff trading accusations of corruption and incompetence, is based on interviews with eight current and former officials involved in the process, most of whom requested anonymity to describe conversations that occurred behind closed doors
The dispute exposed major divisions within the White House over how far to take Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again agenda
Now the future of the UPF definition will signal whether the alliance between MAGA and MAHA can survive

The government’s proposed definition of ultra-processed food has remained largely unchanged since a team led by then – Food and Drug Commissioner Marty Makary first drafted it, in the summer of 2025, according to people close to the process
In about 200 words, it classifies as ultra-processed any food or drink containing a chemical preservative, artificial color, added flavor, or low- or no-calorie sweetener such as stevia and aspartame
Additives intended to thicken foods or otherwise alter their texture, such as guar gum and sodium alginate, will also land a food on the UPF list
The definition relies heavily on existing federal regulations that spell out what, exactly, qualifies as a color, sweetener, or other additive

It excludes infant formula, dietary supplements, and foods that qualify as “healthy” under an FDA standard that sets limits on added sugar, sodium, and saturated fat. (Those products also must contain minimum amounts of healthy ingredients such as fruit and whole grains.) Even with those exceptions, experts we spoke with said, the definition of an ultra-processed food would likely cover most packaged products on grocery-store shelves—not just classic junk food, like cheese-filled pretzel bites, but also many flavored yogurts, instant oatmeals, and protein bars
Most packaged breads, which contain additives that prevent mold and maintain softness, would go on the list too
That’s a frightening proposition to the food industry

The Consumer Brands Association, which represents some of the country’s largest food and beverage manufacturers, including PepsiCo and Tyson Foods, argues that the suspected harms of UPFs—obesity, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer—have not been confirmed by strong scientific evidence
It’s true that the science on UPFs, including which ingredients or processes might make them unhealthy, remains unsettled
But nutrition experts told us that enough evidence links them to poor health outcomes that consumers should be warned
That prospect—that the UPF definition will lead to new regulations and legal actions—has been the crux of the fight inside the administration
Kennedy has advocated for new front-of-package UPF labeling that would be similar to cigarette warnings
The Consumer Brands Association has argued that such a requirement would place an undue burden on food manufacturers

The association has touted a recent study by University of Chicago economists predicting that a mandatory label would prompt food companies to spend billions to reformulate their products, raising the average household’s annual grocery bill by $60
But several nutrition experts we spoke with questioned the study’s assumptions
Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutritional epidemiologist, told us that companies are “reformulating and changing their packaging all the time” and still manage to bring in billions in profit
In fact, some companies have done so recently as part of Kennedy’s push to remove artificial dyes from the American food supply
So far General Mills has voluntarily dropped them from cereals sold in the United States, and Kellogg says it plans to ship reformulated Froot Loops and Apple Jacks by year’s end
Food companies are also concerned that a federal definition might be used in litigation

In the past two years, consumers, as well as the city of San Francisco, have sued major food companies over alleged harmful health effects, and advocates hope that a new definition could make their cases more credible

One attorney, John Morgan of Morgan & Morgan, has been especially active in these suits; his firm previously collaborated with Kennedy on an environmental case and maintained a working relationship with him until he became health secretary
That connection “does raise questions in our mind” about Kennedy’s motivations, Rhonda Bentz, a spokesperson for the Consumer Brands Association, told us

Morgan told us that he doesn’t need a new federal definition to help him make a case against food companies but did not rule out incorporating one. “Their defense is always the same one,” he told us. “It’s deny, delay, deny, delay.” Given how vehemently the food industry opposes these measures, some drama over a government UPF definition was inevitable
But at the beginning of the second Trump administration, the two people at the center of the fight nonetheless believed that they could find a solution

title: You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?
excerpt: Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas
body: Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas
It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other
To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form
Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity: My husband and I are not religious
He’s from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and I grew up attending an interdenominational church, but we don’t attend services now
Lately, though, he’s become so anxious about AI safety and the possibility of human extinction that he’s been having trouble sleeping
In the wake of all this existential uncertainty, he’s expressed a renewed interest in attending church
And he’s not interested in the UU church (with its believe-what-you-want attitude); he said he needs “the strong stuff.”  It’s all a bit mystifying to me because he does not believe in God
But I want him to feel better, and I don’t know what I or anyone can say about AI that will help him manage his anxiety
If religion is what he needs to find solace in the face of radical uncertainty, I want to support him
That said, I have misgivings about attending church myself and about us attending with our kids
I feel a bit self-conscious about being interlopers, and I also feel weird about him going alone every single weekend
More significantly, I wish I understood what the allure is for him
He says he’s hoping it will help him make peace with the end
I’m hoping there is something short of becoming churchgoers we can do that will help him find solace

Dear Secular and Scared, There are a couple of premises I would challenge your husband on, but the idea that religion can be supremely useful in a time like this is not one of them.  In fact, I think this is exactly what religion was made for — and not just because several religions actually grew out of apocalyptic movements (I’m looking at you, Christianity).  Is AI changing your relationship with faith? Tell us about it
Are you turning to faith to navigate your worries about AI? Or are you a religious leader talking with your community about AI? Vox wants to hear from you
Faith has always focused on tackling the biggest moral and spiritual questions of the day
And in our day, lots of those questions center on technology
AI companies are striving to build a machine god , promising it’ll govern our world more intelligently, rationally, and morally than we ever could

Should we welcome that or cling to our own agency ? Which kinds of labor should we outsource to AI, and which should we keep because they’re essential to human dignity? Where does human dignity come from, anyway?  These kinds of questions are the bread and butter of religion
And over the millennia, wisdom traditions of all kinds have had the chance to articulate answers, test and fine-tune them, and develop powerful stories around them that can move people to action
Whether you believe in God or not, I don’t think you need to feel weird about tapping into these wellsprings of wisdom
I think it’s a waste not to.  But there are two points on which I would gently challenge your husband

First, he said he doesn’t want to go to UU because he needs “the strong stuff.” I totally get this impulse — I also find UU services too “anything goes” for my taste — but don’t assume that the stricter a tradition is, the better an answer it has on AI
Most people would consider Catholicism more hardcore than UU
And Pope Leo has strong opinions about AI , many of them great

Yet I actually think he’s fallen into a common “pro-human” trap : trying to argue that there are certain fixed traits that make humans unique, and locating value only in humans as they currently exist

He writes in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas that “ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human.” But that feels insufficient as a guide to the future, because “human” has never been a static category — and it definitely won’t stay one

Instead, religious leaders should be offering us an answer to the question of what we want humanity to become in a tech-augmented world.  Second, your husband seems to be assuming that “the strong stuff” would be church services that help him “make peace with the end.” Services that look the grim reaper straight in the eye and accept that his scythe is coming for all of us, and fast
But it’s not a foregone conclusion that we’ll get an AI takeover resulting in human extinction!  Yes, AI companies are building this technology at a blistering pace
They are gambling with all of our futures as they race toward recursive self-improvement — AIs that can build the next, even smarter AIs themselves
This month, AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano said he now believes there’s “a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years,” meaning that AIs end up calling the shots on Earth
He believes that if we keep building the tech in the fastest, easiest way possible, “we’d be looking at something like a coin flip” — a 50 percent chance of takeover

Others have an even starker view: AI researcher and arch-doomer Eliezer Yudkowsky puts the odds of AI-driven human extinction at 99.5 percent.  But as plenty of experts have pointed out, it’s not clear that AIs will soon be able to outcompete and overpower humans across the board

For starters, AI research can suffer from diminishing returns: The easy discoveries get made first, and then everything you throw at it — more computing power, more experiments, more AI copies — moves things ahead less and less
What’s more, even though AI capabilities improve very fast on well-specified tasks in verifiable domains like math, the real world is messy

So it’s unclear how much their capabilities will generalize to other skills.  And when I investigated the case Yudkowsky makes , I found a lot of assumptions stacked on top of each other: that intelligence is a unitary property you can evenly maximize; that maximizing it in a machine means that machine has so much power it’s tantamount to magic; and that humans will just roll over and let AI grab all the power even as the risks become more glaring
Should we acknowledge that there’s a chance of human extinction here and be appropriately scared of that? Yes
But when faced with a tower of assumptions, of “maybes” and “probablys” that compound, we should not treat extinction as a sure thing

title: Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
excerpt: “When we're playing with a toy, we're often doing something we've never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes
body: “When we're playing with a toy, we're often doing something we've never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen,” Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, tells Vox’s Explain It to Me podcast. | Chen Siyumeng/Xinhua via Getty Images Recently, I was out doing some window shopping with one of my friends
We checked out some of our usual places — a makeup store, a clothing store — but the place where my friend’s eyes really lit up was a toy store
There were floor-to-ceiling displays of Labubus and Funko Pops, Jellycats that looked like croissants, and just about every Hello Kitty product you could imagine
What really got my attention about the space was not the sheer volume of toys, but the lack of kids
It was mostly people our age, with the same excitement that I saw in my friend

This makes sense when you look at a breakdown of the current toy market: It’s an industry projected to be worth over $130 billion worldwide this year, and as of this summer, American adults with no kids bought more games and toys than households with children

There’s even a name for grownups who aren’t ready to put away the toybox: kidults.  According to Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, there’s a reason for our enduring fondness for toys. “The drive to play is actually biologically hardwired into our subcortex,” she told Vox. “Because of that subcortical location, the drive to play actually lasts across the entire lifespan, which means that we’re never too old to play
But our society deeply misunderstands that

We’ve slowly started to take play away as we grow up, and yet that drive is still there.” So what does play actually do for our brains, and how can we add the playfulness of childhood back into our adult lives? We answer that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sundstrom, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545
Adult consumers are making up the lion’s share of the toy industry now
What is happening in our adult brains when we play with toys? Neuroplasticity means that our brains can adapt across our entire lifespan

Some of the similar benefits that children have with playing with toys, we actually still have as adults.  The primary reason is because of the hand-brain connection, which is essentially a two-way neurological highway
When we do fine motor movement while we’re playing with toys, it stimulates the brain regions that are responsible for our cognitive function, our emotion, and our focus

It activates these deep neural networks that go completely unused when we’re engaging in, say, passive screen time.  When we’re playing with a toy, we’re often doing something we’ve never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen

That is actually stimulating new neural pathways in our brain that support our long-term cognitive health.  The second big one is our amygdala, which is a key part of our emotional processing center in our brain, is relaxed in the state of play
A lot of us live in a stress response right now
Social media doesn’t really take us out of that stress response
It often leaves us feeling more stressed out or drained when we’re done.  I absolutely have experienced that.  But that’s not the case with the toys
When we engage in this play state with toys, our amygdala actually calms down
The amygdala is responsible for our stress response

So our stress, our anxiety, our emotional defensiveness are significantly reduced, and we enter that restorative state, which for a lot of us is really hard to access on the day-to-day.  Toys are a pathway to helping us access that more relaxed emotional state based on the reactivity of our amygdala
When do we start being told that we’re too old for toys? What do  we lose when we accept that? Sadly, I think we’re being told that we’re too old for toys starting quite early

Specifically, when we hit the teenage years, a lot of play is replaced with, “If this doesn’t have an immediate purpose for my future career, it’s not worth the time.” That free space to experiment, say, with Lego and even with collections and other things that stimulate our imagination and allow us to enter this world between imagination and reality, starts to slowly dwindle out, almost imperceptibly.  Parents think that they’re doing their children a service by replacing that free play time with structured sports or structured activities

Unfortunately, what happens is, slowly, the intrinsic motivation to do something gets replaced with extrinsic motivation, which very quickly leads to burnout.  It sounds like when we stop playing with toys, that’s when the optimization culture kicks in
We see playing with toys as extra, as a hobby, as something that doesn’t have an immediate purpose toward helping us achieve whatever our goals are

And yet paradoxically, it’s one of the most productive things we can do.  One of the things that I like to ask people is, “Where are you when you get your best ideas?” Now, the shower is the most common answer, but the second most common answer is when they’re playing with toys

You know how no one answers that question? “When I’m at my desk at 10 am answering emails.” The creative mind flourishes in the space in between, and the space in between is the time that is spent playing with toys
But until people see it like that, it becomes really hard to fit into the hustle culture and the grind of the daily schedule

How do we relearn how to play? “Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference.” The first step is to think back on our earliest memories of playing, because play is who we were before the world told us who we have to be
The second, which is a derivative of that, is understanding your own play style
For some people, building a Lego set is going to be totally playful
For other people it’s going to be a puzzle or it’s going to be a game night with a board game or a sports league
And third, this is not about adding more to our plate
Nobody has time for that.  That’s so funny
My first thought is, “I need to put play on my to-do list.” And that is totally contradictory to the purpose of play!  Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference

You can put play objects and toys in visible places around your environment so that you reach for that instead of your phone.  If you just crack the door open a little bit with those micro moments of play in your routine, your brain will automatically enjoy it and start looking for more opportunities to play
Just start really small and know that that’s enough
What do you think the world looks like when adults embrace that playful spirit more? The world looks more joyful

title: Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives will spread lead over part of Iowa – what you need to know about the risks
url:
<title>Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives will spread lead over part of Iowa – what you need to know about the risks</title>
    <content type="html"><p><em>The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it <a href="https://www.army.mil/asc#org-iowa-army-ammunition-plant">confirmed plans</a> to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a <a href="https://www.kcrg.com/2026/11/19/iowa-leaders-lawmakers-react-planned-denotation-ammunition-plant-friday/">few days’ notice</a>. According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing <a href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/61600">lead azide</a>, an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “<a href="https://d34w7g4gy10iej.cloudfront.net/pubs/pdf_77827.pdf">unacceptable risk of accidental detonation</a>.” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.</em></p>

<p><em>However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for miles.</em></p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A rural town with nice houses and a water tower in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773453/original/file-20261122-62-ttggip.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, Iowa, next to a city park. The small town is about 8 miles west of Burlington in southeast, Iowa.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-aerial-view-shows-homes-on-november-20-2026-in-news-photo/2306107359?phrase=middletown%20iowa&amp;adppopup=true">Scott Olson/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><em>The detonations were briefly delayed after the backlash and <a href="https://www.army.mil/article/296926">rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026</a>. A federal appeals court separately <a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ca8.116088/gov.uscourts.ca8.116088.00805660433.0.pdf">paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit</a> for the detonations after two groups sued, but the U.S. Justice Department argued that the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/climate/iowa-lead-plume-ammunition-explosion.html">permit wasn’t necessary</a> in the face of an immediate threat.</em> </p>

<p><em>The Justice Department told the court in a response late on Nov. 21 that the Army <a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/75150222/00805661514/1/iowa-environmental-council-v-epa/">intends to carry out the detonations by Nov. 24, 2026</a>. A precise date and time weren’t immediately released.</em></p>

<p><em>To better understand the risks, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a <a href="https://www.public-health.uiowa.edu/news-items/meet-our-faculty-patrick-oshaughnessy/">professor of occupational and environmental health</a> at the University of Iowa, what people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.</em></p>

<h2>What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people?</h2>

<p>If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/lead-prevention/about/index.html">toxic to humans and pets</a>.</p>

<p>Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The <a href="https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/lead-exposure/lead-exposure-in-children/">big concern there is for young children</a>. If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.</p>



<p>Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2118631119">harm to just about every major organ in our bodies</a>, including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to <a href="https://archive.cdc.gov/www_atsdr_cdc_gov/csem/leadtoxicity/biologic_fate.html">hide out in bones and teeth</a>, where it can leach out and cause harm.</p>

<p>Studies have shown lead exposure is a major <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.reprotox.2023.108342">concern for pregnant women</a> with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abn5164">reduction in IQ</a> in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.</p>

<p>The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/lead-prevention/about/index.html">is no safe level of lead in the body</a>. That’s a pretty strong statement.</p>

<h2>What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel?</h2>

<p>Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.</p>

<p>We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.</p>

<p>In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.</p>

<p><iframe id="N2lV1" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/N2lV1/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Map of plant's location"></iframe></p>

<p>If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, <a href="https://www.army.mil/asc#org-iowa-army-ammunition-plant">the forecast</a> was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.</p>

<p>If the Army goes through with its <a href="https://www.army.mil/article/296772/iaaap_public_advisory">rescheduled plan on Nov. 23</a>, the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.</p>

<p>That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.</p>

<h2>What can people do to stay safe in those areas?</h2>

<p>Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a <a href="https://d34w7g4gy10iej.cloudfront.net/pubs/pdf_78366.pdf">list of precautions</a> that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.</p>

<p>The Army is <a href="https://www.army.mil/article/296772/iaaap_public_advisory">advising people near the plant to vacate their homes</a> during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.</p>

<p>Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.</p>

<p>After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.</p>

<p>Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/farmers-advised-move-shield-livestock-002036349.html">dairy farmers are concerned</a> about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.</p>

<p>Our results from <a href="https://eos.org/research-and-developments/with-little-time-before-lead-azide-detonation-iowa-scientists-and-residents-assemble-monitoring-plans">sampling during and after the plume</a> should help people better understand the risks.</p>

<h2>What is your team planning for testing?</h2>

<p>My <a href="https://www.public-health.uiowa.edu/oeh/">colleagues and I</a> will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.</p>

<p>The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead. </p>

<p>This is all happening last minute – we only found out about the plan a few days before the Army initially planned to detonate the barrels. Thankfully, the university and our <a href="https://www.public-health.uiowa.edu/oeh-research/">federal- and state-funded</a> <a href="https://cheec.uiowa.edu/">centers</a> have the people and technology to quickly carry out testing. We hope to have results about a week after it happens. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also has a team that will be doing sampling.</p>

<p><em>This article, originally published Nov. 21, 2026, has been updated with a Justice Department statement that the Army plans to act by Nov. 24. The date and time were not immediately specified.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297225/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Patrick O&#39;Shaughnessy receives funding from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences</span></em></p></content>
    <summary>An environmental health expert whose University of Iowa team will be testing the air downwind of the detonation site explains the risks people, pets and farms face.</summary>
    <author>
      <name>Patrick O'Shaughnessy, Professor of Occupational and Environmental Health, University of Iowa</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/patrick-oshaughnessy-2779785"
excerpt: Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notic
body: Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice

According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide , an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “ unacceptable risk of accidental detonation .” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined
However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa
People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for miles
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, Iowa, next to a city park
The small town is about 8 miles west of Burlington in southeast, Iowa
Scott Olson/Getty Images The detonations were briefly delayed after the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026
A federal appeals court separately paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations after two groups sued, but the U.S
Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat
The Justice Department told the court in a response late on Nov. 21 that the Army intends to carry out the detonations by Nov. 24, 2026
A precise date and time weren’t immediately released
To better understand the risks, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, what people in the region would face
O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan
What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people? If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe
In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets
Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site
First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles
The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body
The big concern there is for young children
If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths
It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies , including the nervous system and the brain
It tends to hide out in bones and teeth , where it can leach out and cause harm
Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses
In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development
Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body
What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel? Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions
We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks
Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind
In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud
That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air
It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there
If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind
The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north
If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23 , the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast
Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense
We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens
What can people do to stay safe in those areas? Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day
