title: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?
excerpt: Raphael Warnock (D-GA) has kept the door open on a presidential bid. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and t
body: Raphael Warnock (D-GA) has kept the door open on a presidential bid. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and the new Democratic congressional majorities chosen by voters are still more than a month from taking office — but if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary isn’t fully underway, then at the very least, potential candidates are already starting to jockey for position.  Some of that maneuvering was on display earlier this month at the fittingly named “What’s Next” political conference in Denver

The conference drew Democratic operatives, strategists, and presidential hopefuls from around the country — and Vox’s America, Actually podcast, where host Astead Herndon asked attendees for their thoughts about Democratic Party’s future
Herndon also sat down with one possible 2028 candidate: Sen

His background is especially relevant after the midterms: He’s the senior pastor at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta at a time when more Democratic candidates are embracing religious appeals ; and he’s a student of the civil rights movement, the legacy of which could be seen in surging Black turnout across the South after the Supreme Court rolled back parts of the Voting Rights Act
Warnock has kept the door open on a presidential bid ; his colleague Sen
Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is also frequently discussed as a potential candidate

Herndon and Warnock discussed how Democrats can win in the South following election victories by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom and others; why Warnock made the trip to Michigan to campaign for Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed; and the need for presidential leadership to resolve some of America’s toughest problems at home and abroad
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
I feel like some of the reason the South hasn’t seen some of that investment is a presumption that white Southerners are unpersuadable
And in your race, and I think what happened in Georgia, it wasn’t just turnout, but it was also persuasion
It was convincing people to move on from Republicans and embrace Democrats
How do you make that persuasion happen? As a pastor, there’s something that I call the ministry of presence
Sometimes you can’t solve people’s problems because they’re complicated or complex
They may take time, or you may not be able to fix it immediately
But there’s something healing about having people show up for you
And so when I was running in 2021, and then again had to turn around and run in 2022, I would show up in these little towns all across Georgia
The folks were surprised that I was there
And you might be thinking, “Well, of course they were surprised that a Democrat was there.” No, they were surprised that anybody running for the United States Senate was in their little town

And as we sat down and talked about their hospital that had just closed, as we talked about the struggles that their farmers were having under the tariffs that Trump imposed in his first term, we realized that we had things in common, and we shared a faith
And I got enough of those voters to build the kind of moral, multiracial coalition to win
Some of the playbook here, though, feels kind of intuitive
You know, show up, lean in to a kind of shared identity

Campaign everywhere.  Even when I’ve heard Southerners talk about building structures over a long period of time, part of me wonders: Why has it been such an effort to make that happen? Are we talking around racism here? Is it just because these are people who have been written off? That’s a good point, and it’s an interesting thing
Here’s what Black Southerners and white Southerners have in common — particularly poor white Southerners in these rural districts: They’re written off
And if we’re ever to have a moment in this country that transforms it into something that Dr
King called the beloved community, we’ll somehow traverse those boundaries and recognize how much we have in common and how much our interests are connected
I thought it was really interesting how you went to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, who obviously was victorious in that race
I want you to just describe it — why was that advocacy important to you?  First of all, I wanted us to win the majority
But also, as I looked at that debate as it was unfolding, I had to show up
And when we say the Black church, let me hasten because people don’t know this history.  We’ve never meant anything racially exclusive about that
Black church is just a moniker for the anti-slavery church
Because almost all of American Christianity acquiesced — not just acquiesced, aided and provided a kind of moral covering, if you will, for slavery
So the Black church was literally born fighting for freedom

It was born fighting bigotry.  “We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools.” And when I saw the all-out assault on Brother Abdul on the basis of his religious identity — bigotry is bigotry, and religious bigotry is bigotry
The Black church was born fighting bigotry
And so you literally have people saying that he’s unfit because of where he prays and how he prays
And if there was anybody that I felt should be the tip of the spear rejecting that idea, it was the Black church, and so I went, among other things, to remind my colleagues there of who we are
It wasn’t just Republicans who used some of those Islamophobic attacks
There was the infamous scene of Haley Stevens , the Democratic congresswoman who lost that primary, going to the Black church [with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers]

title: The strange, thankless job Chris Van Hollen wants to take from Chuck Schumer
excerpt: Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference at the Capitol on February 2, 2023. | Drew Angerer/Getty Images Sen
body: Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference at the Capitol on February 2, 2023. | Drew Angerer/Getty Images Sen
Chuck Schumer has led the Senate Democratic caucus for 10 years, and he’s now facing the most serious challenge to his post that he’s ever encountered
Just as Democrats are about to take their largest majority since the beginning of Barack Obama’s presidency, Maryland Sen
Chris Van Hollen is challenging Schumer for the role of leading that new majority
Van Hollen has won the backing of several senators so far, as well as various outside progressive groups
In one sense, the reasons Democrats might want to move on from Schumer are obvious
Schumer is 75 years old, and is not a particularly charismatic messenger or compelling speaker
His personal positions on issues like US support for Israel , and his longtime cultivation of Wall Street and corporate donors, put him out of step with the Democratic base
And polls regularly show that he is extremely unpopular
At the same time, the job of Senate majority leader also isn’t really about winning a national popularity contest

It’s about leading the Senate — a challenging remit that involves a multitude of tasks, including but not limited to setting the legislative calendar, crafting legislative and big-picture policy strategy, dealing with outside interest groups, coordinating with the speaker of the House and president, and trying to hold the majority in the next election
And there’s another underappreciated part of the job: volunteering to be the one political figure who’s most likely to be hated

Many of the leaders considered especially effective in their role — from Mitch McConnell to Nancy Pelosi — were consistently unpopular , often because the position requires taking constant slings from both outside and inside their party.  It’s this last component that’s perhaps discussed the least — and in conversations with legislative veterans from across the political spectrum, I’ve been surprised how often it’s come up as a critical part of the case for choosing either of them.  The Senate majority leader’s “heat shield” function How would Van Hollen do the job differently? Publicly, he’s touched on a few points

In first announcing his leadership bid last week, Van Hollen told MS NOW’s Jen Psaki that Democrats should end President Donald Trump’s “illegal and senseless” Iran war this year, by giving Trump a choice: end the war, or the government gets shut down
He said at a conference in Denver that he opposed the Senate filibuster — the rule that requires 60 votes to advance nearly all legislation — and said he would have to “talk to the caucus” about it

And asked by NPR’s Steve Inskeep to name a specific issue in which his approach would be different from Schumer’s, Van Hollen said he would hold a floor vote on the PRO Act , a labor rights bill.  All three positions seem intended to suggest that Van Hollen would try to lead what will be a 56-member Senate caucus in a more progressive direction
But some experts were skeptical about how well that would work. “A leader is like a middleman,” James Wallner, a former Republican Senate aide, told me. “They’ve got to negotiate with everybody
In the Senate we haven’t really seen leaders come from a wing of the party

They usually are going to be dispositionally moderate — and that puts them in a position to negotiate with their own colleagues.” Indeed, current and former Senate leadership aides described the job rather differently — as less about pushing the caucus to do what you want, and more about channeling what senators already want to do, crafting a consensus among them, and serving their needs

Justin Goodman, a former Schumer aide, told me a crucial part of the job was being a “heat shield for the members when difficult decisions need to be made, and they’re difficult decisions the caucus has support for.” The premise here is that much, and perhaps most, of what the Democratic base wants can’t happen

Either because of Trump’s veto pen, the chamber’s rules, or simply because many Democratic senators don’t actually want it to happen — the idea is that many disappointments are inevitable, and that the leader will be the fall guy for them. (Another commonly used term? A “ sin-eater .”) Take, for instance, the PRO Act — which, in 2021 and 2022, the last time Democrats controlled Washington, Schumer did indeed refuse to bring to a floor vote
Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Schumer told him he wouldn’t do it unless Sanders could already line up the 60 supporters necessary to beat the filibuster

The implication is that, if the bill was certain to fail anyway, Schumer did not want to make his vulnerable members take a vote that might be uncomfortable for them — which would expose them to either the base’s fury, or to general election attack ads.  Van Hollen’s professed desire to hold a PRO Act vote would signal a different approach — one that would make progressives happy, and force some moderates to take an uncomfortable vote.  It is not so clear that that approach would be more successful at getting progressive priorities actually signed into law. (And the last time Schumer was majority leader, he did in some instances put moderates on the spot — such as in his push to change Senate rules to pass a voting rights bill, which Sens

Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema voted down.) But Schumer’s most famous example of “sin eating” occurred in March 2025, when he helped orchestrate the passage of a government funding bill, despite progressives’ desire to threaten a shutdown in hopes of fighting back against what they viewed as the new Trump administration’s authoritarian abuses. “I believe so strongly I did the right thing,” Schumer said then . “Nobody wants the government to shut down
But a lot of people don’t want to be the ones to vote ‘yes’ to keep it open,” Goodman told me. “So Sen

Schumer, as the leader, was often the one getting the job done and taking the heat for it.” Schumer later endorsed a more confrontational strategy that resulted in a 43-day government shutdown that fall— but though Democrats were viewed as winning the politics of that fight, some of their members grew increasingly concerned about the pain caused by lapses in government benefits.  Eventually, some Democrats peeled off and voted with the GOP to reopen the government — and though Schumer officially opposed reopening this, he still got blamed for not doing enough to stop it

Has Schumer lost too much credibility to sell these compromises to the base? That said, just because Schumer took on the “sin eater” role in the past doesn’t mean he’s the only one who could do it in the future
It’s possible someone more in touch with the party’s base might be better at finding consensus

Van Hollen is backed by several of the most progressive senators and senators-elect — including Sanders, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota — but he and his supporters have also pushed back against attempts to frame this contest as purely one of progressives versus moderates
Indeed, when I talked to Ezra Levin, co-founder of the progressive group Indivisible, he made a rather different case
Levin argued that, actually, Van Hollen would do a better job at selling the compromises that inevitably will have to be made to the base — including to progressives like him

Levin said he entirely agrees that part of the next leader’s job will be to get the caucus to “do some things that are going to be greatly unpopular” — including funding the government, and raising the debt ceiling. “Senate Majority Leader Chris Van Hollen, if he does his job right, is going to piss off me and other folks a lot,” Levin said

But, he continued, because of Schumer’s history and the longstanding lack of trust in him from the base, Schumer will simply have a harder time selling those compromises.  “If the Senate majority leader is a sponge for anger, you’ve got to change that sponge more than once a decade,” Levin said. “Or that sponge will stop being useful.” Indeed, House Republicans have twice experienced a dynamic like this, where the base’s deep distrust of Speakers John Boehner and Kevin McCarthy resulted in Boehner’s resignation and McCarthy’s ouster
Then, their more conservative successors, Paul Ryan and Mike Johnson, advanced similar legislative compromises without facing serious revolts of their own

Getting a new face really can buy some goodwill and tamp down disquiet, for a time. “If I’m a moderate in the Senate, I want somebody else to take the blame if we do have to push through something,” Levin said. “Who can absorb that blame? Who has credibility with the outside actors? With the grassroots groups blowing up my phone? With all the constituent parts of the Democratic Party?”

title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state

body: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities
Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline
Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday
The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night
Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches
These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days
Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento
Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California
By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains

title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
excerpt: AI keeps getting faster at verifiable tasks — METR's updated report confirms that frontier AI models are doubling their performance on measurable tasks eve
body: AI keeps getting faster at verifiable tasks — METR's updated report confirms that frontier AI models are doubling their performance on measurable tasks every four months
Judgment is where models still stumble — When asked to design new AI evaluations or score philosophical arguments, even the most advanced models fell short of human performance

Some glimmers of progress, but no clean trend lines — A handful of newer models are now scoring "borderline above the bar" on evaluation design tasks, up from "clearly below" just a year ago — though researchers warn these improvements are too sparse to predict where things are headed. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149399" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding
The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used
METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans
Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete
That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled
The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended

One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure

We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures
That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work
It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction
For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them
But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development
And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now

Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two

That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement
METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development
In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results

Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research
In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments
This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D
On this task, too, models fell short of human performance

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own

And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite
Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says

Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well

And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.  Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better
Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising
Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D

METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.  In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming

Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual
It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming
It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment

And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says
But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

title: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death
In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars
In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas
After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck
Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it

Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever

AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?” Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.” It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.” There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet
I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.” To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand
Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables
Read more: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind Inside the stealthy startup that pitched brainless human clones Technology that lets us “speak” to our dead relatives has arrived

Are we ready? <title>Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773223/original/file-20261120-62-73fv9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5168%2C3445&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A &#39;Saturday Night Live&#39; parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-hugging-her-elderly-mother-royalty-free-image/1915738426?adppopup=true"> Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/health/wellness/snl-sister-caregiving-skit-3a6043e4?mod=wknd_pos1">hit home for a lot of people</a>.</p>

<p>The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.</p>

<p>“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.</p>

<p>I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-daunting-economics-of-elder-care-are-about-to-get-much-worse-83123">daunting economics of caregiving for older adults</a> for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.</p>



<h2>A growing trend</h2>

<p>One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.</p>

<p>My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That <a href="https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/ppi/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/caregiving-in-us-2025.doi.10.26419-2fppi.00373.001.pdf">number has since risen to 63 million</a> – about 1 in 4 adults.</p>

<p>The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/valuing-the-invaluable-2026-update/">estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/-X9dxL17t1k?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down</h2>

<p>Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.</p>

<p>Caregiving is tough work, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/01.NAJ.0000336406.45248.4c">numerous studies over the years</a> have found that <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/family-caregivers-health-well-being/">caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress</a> than other people.</p>

<p>That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”</p>

<h2>Family caregivers pay a price</h2>

<p>Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of <a href="https://health.usnews.com/home-care/articles/how-much-do-in-home-caregivers-cost">in-home care is $35 per hour</a>, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a <a href="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MEHOINUSA646N">median annual household income of $87,460</a>. </p>

<p>But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.</p>

<p>Over <a href="https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/ppi/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/hidden-cost-caregiving-lost-earnings-retirement-income-social-security-income.doi.10.26419-2fppi.00433.001.pdf">90% of caregivers must cut their work hours</a>), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. </p>

<p>Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.</p>

<p>AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C15%2C1900%2C1068&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A women with dark hair holds a phone to her ear while sitting in front of a table with prescription bottles." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C15%2C1900%2C1068&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">NBC</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A ‘daughterhood penalty’</h2>

<p>Sociologists have found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122416686521">men with a sister do less parental caregiving</a> than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “<a href="https://www.pbs.org/video/the-daughterhood-penalty-in-americas-caregiving-crisis-qa1c2g/">daughterhood penalty</a>,” or tax. </p>

<p>Social psychologists <a href="https://direct.mit.edu/daed/article/154/1/82/127938/Why-Do-Women-Care-More-amp-Men-Couldn-t-Care-Less">Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught</a> that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.</p>

<p><a href="https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/gender-norms-and-labour-market">Economists’ explanations of gender differences</a> in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, <a href="https://www.proquest.com/openview/6d8960e654bbfcf09490b30f225ac591/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&amp;cbl=1059">economists like me</a> also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.</p>

<p>But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.</p>

<p>Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-024-11191-w">three times more time doing household chores</a> than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297041/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party. </span></em></p></content>

title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy

<title>‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=124%2C0%2C1650%2C1100&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A recent &#39;SNL&#39; sketch called &#39;Sister&#39; lampoons gender roles in caring for aging parents. </span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">NBC</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-X9dxL17t1k">Sister</a>” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?</p>

<p>The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.</p>

<p>According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/caregiving-in-the-us-2025/">63 million Americans provide ongoing care</a> to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YV7PMrEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">researchers</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=WmF6WoIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">who study aging</a>, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geront/gnaf011">initially have better health and financial status</a> than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.</p>

<p>While societal gender expectations help explain why <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/upshot/sister-snl-elder-care.html">daughters often assume the bulk</a> of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/-X9dxL17t1k?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch immediately went viral.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care</h2>

<p>One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/long-term-care">generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance</a> with everyday activities.</p>

<p>Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/home-health-services">Medicare’s home health benefit</a>, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets <a href="https://www.cms.gov/training-education/medicare-learning-networkr-mln/compliance/medicare-provider-compliance-tips/home-health-services">Medicare’s homebound requirements</a>.</p>

<p>This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.71345">national median cost of a home health aide</a> was approximately US$6,688 per month, while <a href="https://www.oasissenioradvisors.com/what-assisted-living/">residing in an assisted living facility</a> averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.</p>

<p>For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that <a href="https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/blog/dual-burden-housing-and-care-older-adults">76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance</a> from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.</p>



<h2>Medicaid can help, but access is limited</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/long-term-services-supports">Medicaid</a>, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.</p>

<p>Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-home-care-hcbs-in-2025/">covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023</a>. The <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/long-term-care-in-the-united-states-a-timeline">divide between these programs dates back to 1965</a>, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.</p>

<p>However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.</p>

<p>Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-look-at-waiting-lists-for-medicaid-home-and-community-based-services-from-2016-to-2026/">spend more than a year on waitlists to get services</a>.</p>

<p>Who provides care in the meantime?</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C318%2C6103%2C3432&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An adult daughter helps her mother walk down a ramp." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C318%2C6103%2C3432&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">As the sketch suggests, daughters are more likely to care for their aging parents.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/senior-headed-down-ramp-to-car-royalty-free-image/2236946401?phrase=daughter%20caregiver&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Visual Vic/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>There’s a shortage of paid caregivers</h2>

<p>Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling <a href="https://kffhealthnews.org/aging/dying-broke-why-long-term-care-insurance-falls-short/">options available through private insurers</a> to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.</p>

<p>The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – <a href="https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/recent-immigration-policies-threaten-sustainability-ltss-workforce">one-third of these workers are foreign-born</a>.</p>

<p>The median hourly wage for <a href="https://www.phinational.org/resource/direct-care-workers-in-the-united-states-key-facts-2026/">direct care work was $17.99 in 2025</a>, only <a href="https://www.visualcapitalist.com/mapped-fast-food-wages-in-every-u-s-state/">$2-$3 per hour</a> more than what fast-food workers earned. </p>

<h2>Caregiving often has financial consequences</h2>

<p>When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.</p>

<p>Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/caregiving-in-the-us-2025/">reduce their income</a> right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.</p>

<p>The federal <a href="https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fmla/family-caregiver">Family and Medical Leave Act</a> provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.</p>

<p>Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.</p>

<h2>Families often have to shoulder responsibility</h2>

<p>Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/state-paid-family-leave-laws-across-the-u-s/">dozen other states</a>, for example, have launched <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0009.12708">paid family leave programs</a>. In <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaids-home-care-support-for-family-caregivers-in-2025/">New York and some other states</a> Medicaid is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/haschl/qxaf192">compensating family caregivers</a>. Washington state is helping <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0009.12439">finance long-term care coverage</a>.</p>

<p>In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris <a href="https://theconversation.com/harris-proposes-that-medicare-cover-more-in-home-health-care-filling-a-large-gap-for-older-americans-and-their-caregivers-240865">proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance</a>, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.</p>



<p>“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.</p>

<p>When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297022/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: A recent 'SNL' sketch called 'Sister' lampoons gender roles in caring for aging parents
NBC A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral

The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free? The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families
According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade
As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers
But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts

While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch immediately went viral

Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities
Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services
However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance

Under Medicare’s home health benefit , limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements
This distinction has enormous consequences
Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home
And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025
For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach
A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses
When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends
Medicaid can help, but access is limited Medicaid , the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer
Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities
The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023

The divide between these programs dates back to 1965 , when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes
Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew
However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state
Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance
Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available
States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services
Who provides care in the meantime? As the sketch suggests, daughters are more likely to care for their aging parents

Visual Vic/Moment via Getty Images There’s a shortage of paid caregivers Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge
The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges
These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born
The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025 , only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned
Caregiving often has financial consequences When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care
Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs
These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future
The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid
And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out
Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks
Families often have to shoulder responsibility Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps
California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states , for example, have launched paid family leave programs
In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers

<title>Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772571/original/file-20261117-78-96a176.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6720%2C4480&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">South Africans prepare to join a convoy in October 2025 to a memorial for white farmers who were victims of violent crimes.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/farmers-prepare-to-drive-in-a-convoy-to-a-memorial-for-news-photo/2239179684?adppopup=true">Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The U.S. State Department <a href="https://www.sabcnews.com/sabcnews/trump-administrations-looks-to-award-near-1m-to-afriforum/">will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum</a>, a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.</p>

<p>The grant, first <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/afriforum-grant-trump-white-south-africans">reported by ProPublica on Nov. 5, 2026</a>, would support research to document the “<a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/bureau-of-democracy-human-rights-and-labor/2026/08/documentation-of-hateful-rhetoric-targeting-minority-populations-in-south-africa">hateful rhetoric and violent acts</a>” experienced by <a href="https://www.nprillinois.org/2025-11-20/who-are-afrikaners-the-group-at-the-center-of-trumps-dispute-with-south-africa">Afrikaners</a> – <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fact-checking-trumps-claims-of-white-farmer-genocide-in-south-africa">descendants of white Dutch settlers</a> who moved to South Africa in the 17th century.</p>

<p>As scholars who study <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=a8EwKzoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">foreign aid</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VYsdAEIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">civil society organizations</a>, we would see U.S. support for AfriForum as a radical departure from the kinds of NGOs <a href="https://www.ned.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2025-Annual-Report.pdf">the U.S. has funded in the past</a>.</p>



<h2>Supporting democracy by funding NGOs</h2>

<p>The U.S. used foreign aid for decades to support efforts to build democracy abroad, enhance governance and <a href="https://2021-2025.state.gov/u-s-achievements-in-advancing-human-rights-globally/">strengthen human rights protections</a>. </p>

<p>Until the second Trump administration, the primary government agencies distributing this assistance were the U.S. Agency for International Development, the State Department and the National Endowment for Democracy. </p>

<p>Past administrations called this assistance “<a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12523">fundamental</a>” to the goals of U.S. foreign policy. By the end of President Joe Biden’s term, funding for democracy promotion had reached almost <a href="https://dx.doi.org/10.1353/sais.2026.a1000457">$3 billion annually</a>.</p>

<p>Some of this money has <a href="https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/09/29/fact-sheet-us-support-civil-society">supported NGOs engaged</a> in civic participation and media independence. These efforts had been particularly important in fragile states and fledgling democracies, where <a href="https://www.ssoar.info/ssoar/bitstream/handle/document/113371/ssoar-2026-gessner_et_al-Backsliding_Democracy_The_Crisis_for.pdf">civil society is especially at risk</a>.</p>

<p>NGOs can also play an important role in reducing risks of violence between different ethnic and religious groups. By raising awareness about past atrocities, they can help <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/pad.1995">stave off future violence</a>.</p>

<h2>Slashing foreign aid</h2>

<p>The Trump administration suspended most <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/reevaluating-and-realigning-united-states-foreign-aid/">U.S. foreign aid in January 2025</a>, soon after Donald Trump was sworn in as president for a second time.</p>

<p>It then <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/07/01/nx-s1-5451372/usaid-officially-shuts-down-and-merges-remaining-operations-with-state-department">dismantled USAID</a>, the federal agency previously responsible for foreign aid and development assistance, and the White House compelled Congress to <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/07/18/nx-s1-5469912/npr-congress-rescission-funding-trumpe">rescind billions of dollars of foreign aid spending</a>. It has continued to take steps in that direction with or <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/14/world/trump-administration-foreign-aid-global-health-diverted-intl">without lawmakers’ cooperation</a>.</p>

<p>As a result, many <a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Into-the-Wood-Chipper/Nicholas-Enrich/9781668226957">lifesaving public health programs</a> lost funding. This policy change has had an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(25)01186-9">enormous human toll</a>, which public health <a href="https://www.impactcounter.com/dashboard?view=table&amp;sort=title&amp;order=asc">researchers have begun to quantify</a>.   </p>

<p>In addition, democracy assistance has been severely cut. <a href="https://carnegieendowment.org/research/2025/03/does-us-democracy-aid-have-a-future">USAID’s Democracy Fund</a>, which funded programs dedicated to building democratic institutions and promoting fair elections and respect for human rights, was eliminated. The Department of State’s and National Endowment for Democracy’s <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/05/29/rubio-human-rights-state-00374606">funding and staffing</a> for <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R49019/R49019.3.pdf">promoting democracy were also slashed</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="President Trump holds a meeting in the Oval Office with a lot of people crowded around." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">U.S. President Donald Trump presents printed news articles to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office in May 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/may-21-2025-us-president-donald-trump-presents-printed-news-news-photo/2215854564?phrase=south%2Bafrica%2Bcyril%2Btrump">Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Claiming there’s a ‘white genocide’</h2>

<p>In our research on NGOs that work on promoting democracy and the prevention of violence, we have seen and documented the <a href="https://ssir.org/articles/entry/preventing-identity-based-violence-in-conflict-zones">benefits of these efforts</a>. The organizations we have studied emphasize how people in South Africa and other countries with a history of identity-based violence can learn to live together across racial, ethnic and religious divides.  </p>

<p>By contrast, <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/afriforum-grant-trump-white-south-africans">AfriForum seeks to lift up Afrikaner identity and history</a>, <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/us-and-foreign-governments-should-be-skeptical-afriforums-lobbying">without any evident effort</a> to bridge the divide between Afrikaners and other racial groups in South Africa. </p>

<p>It champions causes that have contributed to what South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, scholars and other analysts call a false narrative of a “<a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpos.2026.1886481">white genocide</a>” in that country.</p>

<p>In fact, researchers have found that Afrikaners and other white people in South Africa are less likely to be <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cgr5xe7z0y0o">victims of crime</a> and <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cgr5xe7z0y0o">other forms of violence</a> compared to other ethnic and racial groups in South Africa. </p>

<p>By funding AfriForum, the State Department would be elevating the <a href="https://theconversation.com/trump-and-south-africa-what-is-white-victimhood-and-how-is-it-linked-to-white-supremacy-249648">dubious claims the group makes</a> about the oppression of Afrikaners in South Africa.</p>

<p>And <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-american-fixation-on-white-afrikaners-in-south-africa-stretches-back-nearly-a-century-270145">the Trump administration’s embrace</a> of this false narrative goes beyond this grant for AfriForum. It explains why the U.S. has <a href="https://za.usembassy.gov/refugee-admissions-program-for-south-africans/">allowed thousands of white South Africans</a> to come to the U.S. as refugees while denying admission to <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF13277">nearly all other refugees</a> from the rest of the world.</p>
